deep.reconstruction:
Context from the previous page (3r): for two points p, P on the unit sphere at angular distance Δ, Gauss defines f^n(p,P) = (1/π)∫_0^π (cos Δ + i sin Δ cos ψ)^n dψ. This is Laplace's first integral for the Legendre polynomial, so f^n(p,P) = P_n(cos Δ). He reaches it from 1/sqrt(a²+b²) = (1/π)∫_0^π dψ/(a + i b cos ψ). Applied to 1/sqrt(1+u²−2u cos Δ), this gives the generating-function expansion of the reciprocal distance: 1/|kK| = (1/a) Σ f^n(p,P)(A/a)^n, or the same with a and A interchanged. He then divides the unit sphere into infinitely small elements dμ (on 3r called dp), each containing a point p.

This page states two results.

(1) Orthogonality: ∫_{S²} f^m(p,P) f^n(p,P') dμ(p) = 0 when m ≠ n. In modern terms ∫ P_m(p·P) P_n(p·P') dσ(p) = 0 for m ≠ n. The reason, which Gauss does not write: p ↦ P_m(p·P) is a spherical harmonic of degree m, and harmonics of different degree are orthogonal on the sphere.

(2) Reproducing (Funk–Hecke / addition-theorem) formula for equal degrees. Gauss writes ∫ f^m(p,P) f^m(p,P') dμ = (1/((2m+1)π)) f(P,P'), where f(P,P') must mean f^m(P,P'). The correct modern statement, with dσ the area element (total area 4π), is ∫ P_m(p·P) P_m(p·P') dσ(p) = (4π/(2m+1)) P_m(P·P').

Purpose: these are the tools for expanding a function on the sphere, or the potential of a mass distribution, in Laplace series, i.e. spherical harmonics. That fits the 1/r expansion on 3r and Gauss's work on geomagnetism and attraction. No derivation is given on the page; only the statements.
errors: The constant is wrong as written. With dμ the ordinary area element of the unit sphere, the factor should be 4π/(2m+1), not 1/((2m+1)π). The case m=0 shows this: the left side is the total area 4π, while Gauss's formula gives 1/π. Unless dμ carries an unstated normalization (none is indicated on 3r), this is a slip, perhaps a garbled 4π/(2m+1).
The superscript m is missing on f(P,P') on the right-hand side; it should be f^m(P,P').
Neither result is proved on the page. Both are stated without justification.

results.what: f^n(p,P) = (1/π)∫_0^π (cosΔ + i sinΔ cosψ)^n dψ equals the Legendre polynomial P_n(cosΔ), used as coefficients of the 1/r expansion (defined on the previous page)
results.modern_name: Laplace's (first) integral representation of Legendre polynomials; generating function of Legendre polynomials

results.what: ∫_{S²} P_m(p·P) P_n(p·P') dσ(p) = 0 for m ≠ n
results.modern_name: Orthogonality of zonal spherical harmonics of different degree
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace (1782, Théorie des attractions des sphéroïdes); Legendre

results.what: ∫_{S²} P_m(p·P) P_m(p·P') dσ(p) = 4π/(2m+1) P_m(P·P') (Gauss writes the constant as 1/((2m+1)π))
results.modern_name: Reproducing property of zonal harmonics / Funk–Hecke formula; consequence of the addition theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace (late 18th c.); addition theorem formalized by Legendre and Laplace; Funk–Hecke formula 1916/1918

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard Laplace–Legendre facts about spherical harmonics, known from the 1780s. Gauss used Laplace series extensively in 'Allgemeine Theorie des Erdmagnetismus' (1839). A private note restating them, with a slip in the normalization constant, is routine.

checkable.asserts: Reproducing formula for m=1 with correct constant 4π/(2m+1), P=(0,0,1), P'=(sin b,0,cos b) (should be 0)
Reproducing formula for m=2 with constant 4π/5 (should be 0)
m=0 case of Gauss's constant as written: nonzero (4π − 1/π), showing the written constant 1/((2m+1)π) is wrong for the area measure
Generating function 1/sqrt(1+u²-2ux) = Σ P_n(x) u^n through order 4 (should be 0)

transcription_corrections: In the first line the second factor's superscript is n, written over another letter; the transcription f^n is correct.
The measure is written 'dμ' (possibly 'dp' with a stroke); on the previous page Gauss calls the surface element dp.
The right-hand side reads (1/((2m+1)π)) f(P,P') with no superscript on f. The transcription is faithful, but the intended reading is f^m(P,P').
Separators in the arguments vary in the manuscript: '(p.P)' in the first line, '(p,P)' in the second. This has no mathematical significance.
